newsitem.title: UK: UK SOCCER TRIAL HEARS OF HUGE MYSTERY PAYMENTS.
newsitem.headline: UK SOCCER TRIAL HEARS OF HUGE MYSTERY PAYMENTS.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of pounds (dollars) from sources in Asia were paid to a Malaysian alleged to be the middleman in a soccer bribes racket, a British court heard on Thursday.

In a trial that threatens to besmirch soccer's reputation at a time of unprecedented interest in both the finances and flair of the English game, the prosecution alleged a shadowy Asian syndicate sought to corrupt the game at the highest level.
David Calvert Smith, prosecuting at Winchester Crown Court in southern England, said the money paid into the Malaysian's accounts came from Indonesia or Singapore.

He pointed to huge unexplained payments, saying 148,000 pounds ($248,000) was paid in 1991, a further 177,000 pounds ($296,000) was paid in 1992, and tens of thousands more in the following two years.
The money was said to have been received by Heng Suan Lim, 31, who, along with three soccer stars, denies conspiracy to give and accept corrupt payments in order to rig matches.
In the dock with Lim are former Liverpool and Southampton goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, 39, the former Wimbledon striker John Fashanu, 34, and Dutch-born former Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers, 35.
All the defendants in England's first soccer-fixing trial for 30 years have pleaded not guilty. They face up to seven years in jail if convicted.

The prosecution said Zimbabwean-born Grobbelaar -- who won five league titles with Liverpool -- decided to fix the outcome of games after becoming bitter about younger players earning more than him at one of the best European clubs of the 1980s.
The prosecution case is based on telephone bills listing frequent calls between the defendants, especially around match days, and on bank account details, plus covert video and audio recordings.
Calvert Smith said there had been a "steady stream" of telephone calls from Lim to contacts in Indonesia.

"The Crown ask, as it were rhetorically, why, with all this money coming into Lim's accounts from Indonesia and Singapore and with all these telephone calls going out to Indonesia, is there no apparent record of any business at Lim's address which might be behind all this contact with Indonesia," he said.
"If he was exporting trucks or something, or doing some business with the country, you would expect to find invoices, that sort of thing. There is nothing."
He said that, after Grobbelaar had been confronted by newspaper reporters in November 1994 over his alleged involvement in fixing games, contact between Lim and Indonesia tailed away.

"What is the reason for that?" Calvert Smith asked. "If there was some other business going on, a perfectly legitimate and normal business between Mr Lim and the Far East, why does the pattern seem to follow the pattern it does in this case?"
The trial opened on Tuesday and is due to last eight weeks.
